extracted.intended_audience: Victorian general readers; genteel gentlemen musing on professions; readers of humorous/social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: A satirical prospectus / how-to sketch describing the qualities, appearance, and services of two proposed professions (notably a ‘gastronomic agent’/dinner-master) and commentary on the ideal auctioneer. Written as humorous prescriptive advice for would‑be practitioners and their clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pomposity and vulgar titles
rubrics_metrics.description: An auctioneer must avoid an exaggerated notion of himself or his condition; should not ape a higher rank by using grandiose titles (e.g., a bagman styling himself the 'representative' of Dobson and Hobson), nor call his room his 'study' or himself an 'advocate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modest but professional language: 'private room', 'office', or the commonly used phrase among auctioneers. Examples of pomposity include assuming military ranks or inflated job descriptions; these are labelled vulgar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in description and praise
rubrics_metrics.description: The auctioneer must not sacrifice his honesty for his own sake or his clients'; he is not called upon to 'draw the long bow' but to take a favorable, kindly, philanthropic view and say what can fairly be said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise should be genuine and defensible — e.g., writing an eulogium that is 'every word of it true'. Avoid fabrications or excessive puffing on behalf of goods or clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character traits for an auctioneer (psychological profile)
rubrics_metrics.description: The auctioneer should have 'the organ of truth large; of imagination and comparison, considerable; of wit, great; of benevolence, excessively large.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate sincerity, imaginative comparison, wit, and great benevolence; these inner qualities will make the auctioneer persuasive and gentlemanlike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad tasteful knowledge and tasteful speech
rubrics_metrics.description: A genteel auctioneer should be elegantly conversant with lighter literature and able to give a neat history of an author, a sparkling criticism of a work, and an appropriate eulogium on a binding — enough to make non-readers read or at least buy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid meddling with heavy antiquarian and philological works; focus on lighter literature and fashionable tastes so as to speak charmingly about books, pictures, china, jewelry, arms, and antiquities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic enthusiasm for objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The auctioneer must truly feel enthusiasm for the items he sells — he must 'feel them' and not merely affect appreciation; be 'a glass in which all the tastes of fashion are reflected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Become all the characters you address (a 'genteel Goethe or Shakspeare, a fashionable world-spirit') and avoid affectation; authentic feeling persuades buyers more than showy rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and social insight
rubrics_metrics.description: To be the ideal auctioneer one should have had an education in the midst of the best company and an insight into delicate feelings, wants, and usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social intelligence and refined upbringing (or its practical equivalents) are necessary to communicate effectively with fashionable clients and to deliver compelling oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role definition of the gastronomic agent (dinner-master)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gastronomic agent is not a mere provider of meat or wine but a superintendent of the table — an independent expert who looks after the whole art of dinner-giving so the host is not cheated by tradesmen or ignorant of proper service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position the agent as a consultant and guarantor of quality rather than a retailer; his value is in expertise and impartial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hiring a ruined gastronomist (integrity requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not select a ruined gastronomist as table-master because the opportunities for peculation would be too great; a ruined man might be bribed or make bargains with tradesmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer financially stable, reputable agents to reduce risk of collusion, bribery, or misappropriation of supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of male professional for dinner-giving (satirical social claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay claims (satirically) that women, as a rule, are bad dinner-caterers — 'they are children in the gormandizing way' — and that great dinners must be organized by a (male) professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the author's comic axiom; in practical terms the guidance is to appoint a dedicated, knowledgeable professional rather than rely on amateur household managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for social standing and affectation of rank
rubrics_metrics.description: The agent should be as high-born as possible or at least able to tack an honorable handle to his name; display of rank on professional cards (honorifics, Gothic letters, coat-of-arms) persuades clients and brings business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social signals (titles, elegant cards, gilt elements) to convince clientele that the agent moves in the 'best society' and is therefore fit to advise them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional mise-en-scène and French affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The agent's chambers should be handsomely furnished, opened by a French valet, contain a library of cookery and wine books under plate-glass, sample bottles/truffles on display, busts of famous cooks, and framed menus of great dinners — and the agent should use French terms in speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create an appearance of cultivated, Continental expertise; the setting and use of French are meant to impress the 'vulgar' but should be credible and consistent with professed expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal appearance and comportment
rubrics_metrics.description: The agent should appear portly and grave, wear a dark dress, an enormous gold chain, a large diamond ring, carry a gold snuff-box — a dignified Canning-like figure — and employ manners that command respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a look and manner that signal authority and tasteful wealth to reassure clients of competence and status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification: ancestral pedigree of good living
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent should be 'of one of the best families in England' and able to claim ancestral association with gastronomic innovations (e.g., ancestors who introduced peacock roast or gooseberry sauce).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use asserted family traditions of good living as part of a persuasive professional narrative (the prospectus explicitly encourages such claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification: lifelong devotion to the study of the table
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent should have devoted his life to no other study than that of the table and visited the courts of Europe, taking receipts of cooks and living in intimacy with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate practical apprenticeship and continental experience; present collected recipes and personal relationships with skilled cooks as credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification: intimate knowledge of vintages
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent must have the same acquaintance with continental vintages (Johannisberg, Bordeaux, Oporto, Xeres) from personal travel and observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming specific vintage knowledge and vintage-season experience is part of the expertise clients expect; cite years/places to create credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification: practical market and fish/meat expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent should have attended purchases with established suppliers (e.g., Mr. Groves, Mr. Giblett) and be able 'at a glance' to recognize the age of mutton, primeness of beef, and firmness/freshness of fish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop hands-on procurement skills and supplier contacts; practical recognition of product quality is essential for the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification: field visits to parks and gardens
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent should have visited parks, grouse-manors, and principal gardens of England to evaluate produce professionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field knowledge of game, poultry, and produce sources supports menu planning and procurement claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service: provision of trustworthy cooks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent, through his subordinates, engages to provide cooks to dress dinners — a list of cooks he will recommend 'none who are not worthy of the strictest confidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a vetted roster of reliable cooks and only recommend those of unquestionable character and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service: menu tailored to price
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent will provide 'a menu for the table, according to the price which the Amphitryon chooses to incur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer menus scaled to clients' budgets and make clear what is appropriate at each price point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service: sourcing viands and international correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Through correspondence with metropolitan fournisseurs (and Paris when needed), the Agent will provide viands, fruit, wine, etc., leveraging foreign contacts (e.g., Messrs. Chevet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use supplier networks, including international sources, to secure superior ingredients; present this as part of the service promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service: provision/listing of dexterous table-waiters and servant control
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent will provide a list of dexterous table-waiters (humor: all answering to the name of John) and recommends that the household servants be locked in the back-kitchen during the dinner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply experienced front-of-house staff and control in-house service to ensure consistency; practical protocols for staffing should be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service: auditing fournisseurs' accounts and refusing gratuities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent will receive and examine all accounts of the fournisseurs, pledging his honor not to receive paltry gratifications, and to ensure bills are moderate and goods of better quality than less experienced clients would secure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent account auditing and a written pledge against kickbacks; this is a key trust-building measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service: fixed fee and restrictions on client interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent's fee for superintending a dinner will be five guineas; clients are urged to trust the Agent entirely and not to insert dishes or wines of their own without prior consultation (samples for wine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charge a clear fixed professional fee and require that clients submit special requests in writing or samples to prevent last-minute alterations that jeopardize the ensemble of the dinner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service: consultation hours and importance of personal interview
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent will be at home for consultation from ten until two (earlier if needed) and emphasizes that a personal interview is best to ascertain the number and character of guests, their tastes, health, rank, and profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule clear consultation windows and insist on personal meetings to tailor menus and service to guest profile and sensitivities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service: rounds schedule and area coverage; refusal to serve palaces
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent will conduct rounds in specified districts with precise time windows (e.g., 2–3 Russell Square; 3–3¾ Harley Street; etc.) and peremptorily announces he will NOT go to the palace, where it is impossible to serve a good dinner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a predictable visitation schedule for client convenience and set explicit boundaries on venues where quality cannot be assured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradesmen engagement: weekly trial-dinners and supplier competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Monday evening in season the Agent proposes trial-dinners (covers for ten) supplied gratis by selected tradesmen and cooks; wine‑merchants will compete by sending their best samples and leaving price tickets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use curated trial dinners to vet suppliers, create competition among vendors, and keep records (a supplier book) so quality can be demonstrated and preferred suppliers chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradesmen accountability: receipts and strict judging
rubrics_metrics.description: The maitre-d'hotel will give a receipt to each supplier for the articles produced, the Agent is presented as a 'VERY KEEN JUDGE', and poor service will be punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute a system of receipts and written accountability for suppliers; apply rigorous judgment and communicate consequences for substandard performance.
